Q: How to parse informal Persian number words into an integer currency value (Rial) A:

Dictionary size is actually quite manageable:
Root number words: ~30-40 words
Ones: یک, دو, سه... (1-19) ≈ 19 words
Tens: بیست, سی, چهل... (20-90) ≈ 8 words
Hundreds: صد, دویست, سیصد... (100-900) ≈ 9 words
Multipliers: هزار, میلیون, میلیارد, تریلیون ≈ 4 words
Common typos/variants: ~20-30 additional forms
"هزا" / "هراز" for "هزار" (thousand)
"پونصد" / "پتنصد" for "پانصد" (five hundred)
"هتصد" for "هفتصد" (seven hundred)
"ملیون" for "میلیون" (million)
Total: ~60-70 entries - very manageable!
Composition rules are minimal:
Persian number composition is actually quite straightforward compared to its other agglutinative features:
Addition within scale: "سی و پنج" (30 and 5) = 35
Multiplication by scale: "پنج هزار" (5 thousand) = 5,000
Chaining scales: "دو میلیون سیصد هزار" (2 million 300 thousand)
The real complexity isn't linguistic - it's user behavior
Missing spaces: "ملیونپانصد" (million+five-hundred stuck together)
Mixed formats: "108 هزارو 6" (digit + word + word)
Implicit context: "یک میلیون و 150" means 1,150,000 (the 150 is implicitly in thousands)
Inconsistent currency mixing: "100 تومن و 58 ریال" (needs special handling)
So the challenge is less about Persian morphology and more about parsing informal, inconsistent user input where they mix conventions.

Q: Apache NIFI - Fail to insert using PutDatabaseRecord: Record does not have a value for the Required column 'name A:

I have figured out the error after investigating for 6 days. The problem was in the CSV file. It was written with ";" semicolon when I changed it to "," comma it worked perfectly.

before:

name;age;email
john doe;56;u@gmail.com
hamed;25;fff@gmail.com
arjun;55;ru@gmail.com
ali;21;ffuty@gmail.com
saleh;16;djh@gmail.com

After:

name,age,email
john doe,56,u@gmail.com
hamed,25,fff@gmail.com
arjun,55,ru@gmail.com
ali,21,ffuty@gmail.com
saleh,16,djh@gmail.com

Q: AWS RDS IOPS v Aurora IOPS A:

With Aurora, you pay a certain rate (which varies depending on the AWS Region) per million I/O operations. So you would estimate how many IOPS you really experience and plug that into the pricing calculator. I presume the 3000 IOPS from RDS was the maximum you could ever need during the busiest peak, not the amount that was really happening 24x7x365.

You can see here the network bandwidth limits for Aurora depending on the instance class:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Concepts.DBInstanceClass.html#Concepts.DBInstanceClass.Summary

I am a big fan of the recently announced I/O-optimized configuration:

https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2023/05/amazon-aurora-i-o-optimized/

It bakes the price of the I/O into the charges for instance hours and storage, which are easier to predict. So it's cheaper for a busy cluster that otherwise would have lots of I/O charges, although not as good a deal for a relatively lightly used cluster. (But you can switch from I/O-optimized back to the traditional I/O billing with no downtime.)

Q: MySQL phpMyAdmin: Error #1932 - Table doesn't exist in engine A:

Same happened to me in Windows, lost my old course databases after uninstalling old version and installing new one. When you uninstall the old version of xampp, even though it lets you save the htdocs and mysql/data folder, it will remove the ibdata1 file from there. So after you uninstall, even though you still have all the databases folders in mysql/data now that you lost the corresponding ibdata1 file, they are now useless. Copying a new ibdata1 file from the new installation of xampp will not solve this. Basically there is no way to go back. This could have easily been avoided if the Xampp uninstaller would not have touch the mysql/data folder at all, leaving it to the user to procced, instead of removing few files there and making its content irrelevant after.

But the way how I was able to restore the DB was by using a SQL script file of the entire database with the data inserted on tables (I had one as a backup option to quickly recreate the db from scratch).
